newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Sages of "The Way" hail Hong Kong transfer to China.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sages of "The Way" hail Hong Kong transfer to China.

text.p: The Taoist sages of Hong Kong have consulted temple oracles about the July 1 transition to Chinese rule. It's a good idea, they say, so eat, drink and be merry -- within reason, naturally.
Western New-Age followers of the Tao (the Way), the ancient Chinese creed of world-shunning passivity, could get a shock in meeting the priests here.
These are truth-seekers, too, but in a worldly way. They are wealthy businessmen in double-breasted suits who look more like Rotarians, except when robed for rituals.

As Hong Kong prepares to rejoin China after 156 years of British rule, Taoists plan jubilations that mix days of prayers with nights of feasting, a combination fully in line with their far-from-ascetic image.
Their announcement was made at a news conference and reception that had all the slickness of a trading conglomerate announcing a new share issue.
"It is right to celebrate," says Tong Kwok-wah, chairman of the Hong Kong Taoist Asssociation. "What was taken from China is now returning to the motherland."
What of Taoists, targeted by Chinese communists for suppression in the past, who may not see the issue in that light? A slight gesture waves the question away.

With a faint air of wizardry, Tong is a slightly built, elderly man who says very little. Surrounded by aides intent on his every word, he exudes a sense of power. His business card shows he is a tycoon who heads half a dozen companies.
Asked if there was a contradiction between riches and the Tao, he says: "It depends. Everything in moderation. We have to make a living."
UNITY MAY BE GOOD BUSINESS AS WELL

The local Taoists' acclaim for unity with China may be a shrewd decision as much as a spiritual one, reflecting an extraordinary surge in business community confidence by all the usual market indicators.
Books about the Tao tend to convey an impression of hermits cultivating self-denial in the mountains of China.
That sounds far too difficult for crowded, bustling Hong Kong, an ultra-capitalist bastion where fast-buck doctrines like "greed is good" are never questioned.
The Taoist leaders here are more fully in tune with the message from China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, in launching mainland economic reforms: "To be rich is glorious."
The universal question, finding the right way in life, the Tao -- the Chinese pronunciation is Dao as in the English "how"-- is clearly a subjective matter.
The Taoists coexist in Hong Kong with China's other major religion, Buddhism, along with ancestor worship strongly influenced by Confucianism, more a moral code of behaviour than a faith.

Hong Kong's other religious groups, which include Jews, Moslems, Christians, Hindus and Sikhs, have not been so forthright about joining officially atheist, communist-ruled China, preferring a wait-and-see attitude.

Tong says his followers will stage large banquets and a Taoist ritual assembly for seven days in July "praying for the well-being of Hong Kong's future" when he and his fellow-priests will don their black, box-shaped hats and colourful robes.
IN SECULAR AGE, MOST PRIESTS ARE PART-TIMERS
In this secular age, he says, most clerics are part-time, except for a few monks in Taoist monasteries attached to temples where followers worship in a hectic, incense-laden atmosphere.
Hong Kong has about 600 temples of all kinds. The Taoist Association, set up in 1961, has 60 group members and 700 individual members.
But Tong says about one-third of Hong Kong's 6.4 million population has some belief in Taoism, which is more than 4,000 years old.
Classical Taoism, which has gained adherents outside Asia, arose from philosophy and proffers some tantalising questions in a book by Lao Tzu, "Tao te Ching" (The Way and the Power.)
Many people have been attracted and puzzled by a central tenet of its passivism -- take no action, so avoiding an unknown influence on events. That's not quite the Way here.

Tong's news conference, launched by an American-style public relations firm with glossy books and statements, was held in a plush restaurant in Kowloon's huge Dragon Centre shopping mall, a monument to in-your-face consumerism that the Chinese like.

At a reception, white-gloved waiters handed round snacks and drinks. Recorded military marching music boomed out. Inside the centre's massive nine-storey-high atrium, a roller-coaster ride twisted and dived, with child passengers screaming in delight.
